title: Science and doubt
goals: Use the reporting passive (It is believed that…, is thought to have…) with the appropriate tense form.
Build passives with two-object verbs and prepositional verbs, choosing the subject with judgement.
Use the causative have/get something done for services and experiences.
Decide when the passive is appropriate in scientific texts, and form its tenses and modals.
Talk about findings with academic caution and assess evidence using vocabulary of doubt.
Write a short report and an opinion essay in a formal, nuanced register.

learn.title: Reporting passive: It is believed that… / is thought to have…
learn.html:
It is the star structure of scientific and journalistic English for presenting ideas that circulate without personally committing to them. It is the English counterpart of the impersonal “it is believed that…” style, but it has two constructions and a finer system of tenses.

StructureExampleUse
It + is believed / thought / said / known / estimated / expected + that + clauseIt is believed that the virus spread through contact.Impersonal, very formal
Subject + is believed + to + infinitiveThe virus is believed to spread through contact.Same time or future
Subject + is believed + to be + -ingResearchers are thought to be working on a vaccine.Action in progress
Subject + is believed + to have + past participleThe planet is thought to have formed 4.5 billion years ago.Earlier action
There + is believed + to beThere is thought to be a link between sleep and memory.Existence

Nuances:

  • Common verbs: believe, think, say, know, consider, understand, expect, estimate, report, assume, suppose, allege, find, show. With hope only It is hoped that… exists; with suggest, you say It has been suggested that… (not «he is suggested to»).
  • The choice between to do / to be doing / to have done marks the time relation with the reporting verb: simultaneous, in progress or earlier. This is what costs Spanish speakers the most, because they tend to use a single form for every time.
  • With negation or greater distance: is not known to have…, is widely believed to…, is now thought to…
  • In science, widely, generally, now, previously place the degree of consensus: It was long believed that…, but it is now known that…
  • Compare with Unit 3: there you reported what someone said; here the focus is on the idea, and who holds it is omitted or blurred.

watch.wrong: The patient is believed that he has recovered.
watch.right: The patient is believed to have recovered. / It is believed that the patient has recovered.
watch.why: With a personal subject: passive + to-infinitive; do not mix it with that.

watch.wrong: The dinosaurs are thought to die out 66 million years ago.
watch.right: The dinosaurs are thought to have died out 66 million years ago.
watch.why: Earlier event: to have + past participle.

watch.wrong: There is thought to being a link.
watch.right: There is thought to be a link.

watch.wrong: It is said to that the drug works.
watch.right: It is said that the drug works. / The drug is said to work.
watch.why: Do not combine to with that.

learn.title: Passive with two-object verbs and prepositional verbs
learn.html:
Verbs such as give, offer, send, show, tell, award, grant, promise, teach, pay, lend have two objects (indirect: the person; direct: the thing). That is why they allow two passives:

ActivePassive A: person as subjectPassive B: thing as subject
They awarded her the prize.She was awarded the prize.The prize was awarded to her.
The lab offered us a grant.We were offered a grant.A grant was offered to us.

Passive A is the preferred one in English because it usually matches the topic of the sentence (we start with whoever matters to us). Passive B is necessary when you want to put the person at the end (new information), or when the verb does not allow A.

Verbs that only allow the passive with the direct object (the person takes to): explain, suggest, describe, announce, mention, say, report, propose. The theory was explained to us (not «we were explained the theory»). This is a very common calque, since Spanish does say «nos fue explicada».

Passive with prepositional verbs: the preposition stays with the verb: The results were looked into. The proposal was argued against. The patient is being taken care of. This is common in reports, and the preposition must not be «lost».

by-agent: it is added only when it is informative (The study was funded by a charity), and at the end of the sentence, following the principle of end-focus.

watch.wrong: The solution was explained us by the professor.
watch.right: The solution was explained to us by the professor.
watch.why: Explain does not take the person as the passive subject.

watch.wrong: She was suggested a different approach.
watch.right: A different approach was suggested to her.

watch.why: Look at keeps its preposition in the passive.

watch.wrong: The truth was never told the public.
watch.right: The truth was never told to the public.
watch.why: With the thing as subject, the person takes to.

learn.title: have / get something done (causative)
learn.html:
The causative structure expresses that someone does something for us (a service), or that something happens to us without our doing it. It is formed with have / get + object + past participle: I had my laptop repaired. Spanish has no direct equivalent for this, so the structure is often mistranslated word by word.

StructureExampleNuance
have + obj + past participleShe had her paper reviewed by two experts.Neutral / slightly more formal
get + obj + past participleI need to get my passport renewed.More colloquial; sometimes implies effort
have + person + bare infinitiveShe had her assistant book the flights.Telling someone to do it
get + person + to + infinitiveWe got the lab to repeat the test.Persuading or managing to get them to do it
have / get + obj + past participle (unpleasant experience)He had his bike stolen.Something that happens to us
get + past participle (passive with get)He got caught cheating.An event, often unexpected

Nuances:

  • The same form had his car stolen is ambiguous between “his car was stolen” (an experience) and “he arranged for it to be stolen” (not very plausible); context almost always makes clear that it is a misfortune.
  • With have + person, to is not used: had him check, never had him to check.
  • The agent is added with by only when it matters: had the thesis proofread by a professor.
  • The causative works with tenses and modals: I'm having the kitchen redone. You should get that checked.

watch.why: Direct past participle, without to be.

watch.right: She had her assistant book the flights. / She got her assistant to book the flights.
watch.why: Have + person + base; get + person + to.

watch.right: I had my hair cut yesterday at the salon.
watch.why: If someone else did it for you, use have + past participle.

watch.wrong: He had stolen his wallet on the bus.
watch.right: He had his wallet stolen on the bus.
watch.why: The order object + past participle expresses that it happened to him.

learn.title: The passive in scientific writing: when and how
learn.html:
The passive is not “more formal” in itself: it is a decision about focus. In academic and scientific texts it is chosen when what matters is the action or the result, not who did it.

  • Unknown or irrelevant agent: Samples were collected at baseline. (it does not matter who)
  • Focus on the procedure: Methods sections: The mixture was heated to 80°C and stirred for ten minutes.
  • Cohesion: start with information that is already known and leave the new information for the end (end-focus): The trial was designed by a team led by Dr. Reyes.
  • Distance and objectivity: avoid repeated “I/we” in formal reports.

Forms you must master:

FormExample
Passive present continuousThe drug is being tested on volunteers.
Passive present perfectThe results have not been published yet.
Modal + be + past participleThe findings should be interpreted with caution.
Passive modal perfectThe error could have been avoided.
need + to be + past participle / need + -ingThe hypothesis needs to be tested again. / needs testing.

Caution: too many passives make the text heavy and ambiguous (who concluded?). If the agent matters, use the active (The authors conclude that…). Also avoid the passive with intransitive verbs (happen, occur, rise), which have no passive.

watch.wrong: The results can explain by several factors.
watch.right: The results can be explained by several factors.

watch.wrong: The bridge is building at the moment.
watch.right: The bridge is being built at the moment.
watch.why: Present continuous passive: is being + past participle.

watch.wrong: The accident was happened last night.
watch.why: Happen is intransitive: it has no passive.

watch.right: The data haven't been analysed yet.
watch.why: Present perfect passive: have been + past participle.

learn.title: Talking about findings with academic caution
learn.html:
• The findings point to… / are consistent with… — presenting results without claiming them as proof.
  • Further research is needed to establish whether… — acknowledging limits.
  • These results should be interpreted with caution. — warning about limitations.
  • It remains to be seen whether… — leaving the question open.
  • This is not to say that… / That is not to suggest that… — qualifying a possible conclusion.
  • On the face of it, … however, … — “at first sight”; introduces a reservation.
  • A word of caution: … / One caveat is that… — pointing out a limitation.
  • It is too early to say… — avoiding premature conclusions.

write.prompt: Write a short report of 250 to 350 words about a study (real or invented) in which you present the findings with academic caution. Use at least three reporting passives (is thought to have…, It is believed that…), one causative, and vocabulary from v-science and v-research-verbs. Possible opening: A recent study, which was carried out by…
checklist: 250–350 words with a report structure (context, method, findings, limitations)
At least 3 reporting passives with the correct tense form (to be / to be -ing / to have + past participle)
At least 1 causative (have/get + obj + past participle)
At least 5 words from v-science / v-research-verbs
One limitation with a caveat, tentative wording, or “should be interpreted with caution”
write.model:
A recent study, which was carried out by a team of sleep researchers at a European university, examined the relationship between screen use and sleep quality in teenagers. Adolescents today are generally thought to be sleeping less than previous generations, and previous research is believed to have underestimated the effect of evening screen exposure. The authors therefore set out to test this hypothesis more rigorously.

The sample consisted of 480 adolescents aged between fourteen and seventeen. Participants were recruited from twelve schools and were asked to wear a wristband that recorded their sleep for four weeks. Screen time was measured with an application installed on their phones, and each participant had their blood pressure and body mass checked at the start and at the end of the study. The data were then analysed by an independent statistician, whom the team had hired to reduce bias.

The findings are striking. Teenagers who used screens for more than two hours after 9 p.m. were found to sleep, on average, forty minutes less than those who did not. A significant correlation was also observed between late screen use and lower exam performance. Blue light is thought to have disrupted the production of melatonin, although this mechanism was not directly tested. It is widely assumed that the effect is causal, but the results do not prove it.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The sample was drawn from urban schools only, and sleep was partly self-reported, so the results may not be representative of all adolescents. Moreover, the study was not designed to control for variables such as caffeine consumption or family stress. The conclusions should therefore be interpreted with caution, and further peer-reviewed research is needed before any firm recommendations are made.

In summary, the study suggests, rather than demonstrates, that evening screen use is associated with poorer sleep.

write.prompt: Write an opinion essay of 250 to 350 words: «Should news headlines about science be treated with scepticism?». Contrast what a headline says with what the study probably says; use passives with two-object verbs and vocabulary of doubt.
checklist: 250–350 words with an introduction, arguments and a conclusion
At least 2 passives with two-object verbs (was awarded, was offered, was explained to…)
write.model:
Last month, a headline announced that "Coffee Cures Memory Loss". Readers were promised a miracle in a cup. The study behind it, however, seems to have said something far more modest. On the whole, I believe science headlines deserve a healthy dose of scepticism, though not cynicism.

The first reason is that headlines are written to attract readers, not to inform them. A researcher who has been offered a few lines in a newspaper is rarely given the chance to explain the limits of her work. In the coffee example, the participants were given either a coffee or a placebo and were asked to complete a memory test; the difference was small, and it was observed in only forty volunteers. The study probably claimed no more than a tentative association, but the headline presented it as a cure. It would appear that every layer of reporting makes the findings sound more certain than they are.

A second reason is that dubious claims spread faster than careful ones. Questionable results are shared thousands of times before a correction is ever published, and unfounded fears can last for decades. A far-fetched claim repeated often enough begins to sound plausible.

Nevertheless, scepticism should not become blanket distrust. Some journalists do an admirable job, and several of the most important discoveries of recent years were explained clearly to the public by science reporters. The sensible approach, in my view, is to ask a few questions: who funded the study, how many people were involved, and whether the result has been replicated. The evidence suggests that these simple checks filter out most of the exaggeration.

In conclusion, headlines should be taken with a pinch of salt, but not thrown away. Readers who were never taught to question what they read are easy to mislead; those who are encouraged to do so will find that good science can still be recognised beneath the noise.

reading.title: Coffee, correlation and the trouble with headlines
reading.intro: Read the text about how scientific findings are communicated and answer the questions.
paragraphs: Every few months, a headline announces that a common food or habit has been shown to prolong life, or, just as confidently, to shorten it. Red wine is said to protect the heart one week and to damage the liver the next. For readers who simply want to know what to eat for breakfast, the effect is bewildering, and it is hardly surprising that many have concluded that scientists cannot make up their minds. The truth, however, is rather different: the science is usually far more cautious than the coverage it receives. Researchers rarely claim to have settled a question; they report what a particular group of people showed under particular conditions, and they say so in careful, deliberately modest language.

Consider a typical case. A team of researchers followed 40,000 adults for twelve years and found that those who drank three cups of coffee a day were less likely to die during the study period than those who drank none. In the original paper, the authors stated that coffee consumption "was associated with" lower mortality and explicitly warned that the results should be interpreted with caution. Participants had been asked to report their own habits, which are notoriously unreliable, and people who drink no coffee at all may well have been advised to avoid it for health reasons in the first place. By the time the study had been summarised in a press release, however, the wording had been simplified to "coffee adds years to your life", and within hours that claim had been repeated by dozens of websites.

What went wrong is not mysterious. Most scientific findings are, by their nature, provisional. A single study, particularly one with a modest sample size, is generally regarded as a starting point rather than a conclusion. Its results need to be replicated by independent teams, and its methods subjected to peer review, before it is accepted as part of the body of knowledge. Even then, the distinction between correlation and causation remains easy to overlook. Two things that rise and fall together are not necessarily connected; a third factor, such as income or lifestyle, may account for both. Researchers therefore tend to rely on carefully chosen verbs. A finding "suggests", "is consistent with" or "points to" something; only rarely does it "prove" anything.

Journalists are not entirely to blame. They are under pressure to attract readers, and a nuanced sentence rarely goes viral. Universities, too, have their share of responsibility, since their press offices are often keen to have their institution's work noticed. Yet readers are far from powerless. A few habits can be acquired quickly: checking whether a study was conducted on humans or on mice; asking how many people were involved; looking for phrases such as "may", "could" and "is associated with"; and being sceptical of any headline that contains the word "breakthrough". Above all, it helps to remember that doubt, far from being a weakness of science, is the mechanism by which it corrects itself. A discipline that never admitted uncertainty would be one that had stopped learning.

listening.title: Is it really a breakthrough?
listening.intro: Listen to the radio programme with three voices. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Welcome back to The Open Lab. Today we're asking whether a recent breakthrough in sleep research is as exciting as the headlines suggest. With me are Dr. Chen, who led the study, and Dr. Ibarra, who is rather more sceptical.
Thanks for having us. I should say at the outset that we never used the word breakthrough. Our paper reports that people who slept less than six hours were found to have slightly worse memory scores.
But the press release said that poor sleep destroys your memory.
Yes, and I had the wording changed before it went out, but apparently the university's communications team had already sent a draft. It's rather frustrating.
My concern is the sample. Only ninety volunteers were recruited, and most of them were students. Whatever the findings suggest, they can hardly be generalised to the whole population.
That's fair. We make that point in the discussion section. The results are thought to be indicative, not conclusive.
So what would make the result more convincing?

Replication, above all. If another lab were to get the same pattern with a larger, more diverse group, I'd be a lot more persuaded. It's also worth asking whether the participants were simply stressed. Stress could well account for both the poor sleep and the poor scores.
Which is why we had every participant's stress levels assessed beforehand. The effect, such as it is, remained after we controlled for that.
Fair enough, I hadn't noticed that. Then I'd say the finding is promising, but I'd still treat it with caution.
Dr. Chen, what's next for your team?
We've been awarded funding for a three-year follow-up, so we're going to have the whole protocol reviewed by an independent panel before we start.
Good news. And what's the moral for listeners?
Read past the headline. If an article says a study proves something, be wary. Real research usually says suggests.
And sleep well in the meantime, whatever the data say.
